seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, while the Meade basin still holds continuous firm snow and before the steep summit snowfield thins over loose rubble

June.reason: Road to Conrad Meadows is usually passable, but Conrad Creek runs high and deep snow makes the upper approach slow and avalanche-exposed.

July.reason: The Meade basin is a continuous, firm snow climb with crampons, snowbridges still hold over creeks and moats, and camps near Conrad Creek have water.

August.reason: The basin usually still holds snow, but the steep snowfield below the summit scramble softens and thins, and moats open at the glacier edges.

September.reason: Snow melts back to hard, thin patches over loose rubble with bad runouts, the summit scramble is looser, and water on the long approach gets scarce.

October.reason: First storms put fresh snow on icy old snow and loose rock, days are short for a 20-mile round trip, and the approach road can close with early snow.

September.reason: Dry ribs, fewer summer crowds at the Snowgrass camps and stable weather; late-season snow patches can be hard and icy in shaded gullies early in the day.

October.reason: Early storms dust the loose breccia with snow and verglas, days are short for the long traverse, and the high access roads can close after the first heavy snow.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, after the steep southwest face melts to heather and before fall snow returns to the saddle

May.reason: The trail above treeline is still snow-covered and the 40-50 degree southwest face is a loaded avalanche slope; few parties summit before the snow recedes.

June.reason: Deep snow from the shoulder into the saddle; firm mornings allow step-kicking with axe and crampons, but afternoon slush on the face is hazardous.

July.reason: Snow on the trail melts quickly, while consolidated snow on the southwest face gives secure step-kicking with an axe; wildflowers peak in the meadows.

August.reason: The face has mostly melted to heather and rock, so the diagonal traverse goes without crampons; carry water since snowmelt sources dry up.

September.reason: Snow-free heather and rock on the face, fall color in the meadows and cooler temperatures for the long 3,200 ft climb to the shoulder.

October.reason: First snows and frozen heather on the steep southwest face make the traverse slick, and daylight is short for the off-trail descent from the saddle.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: March through April, when a consolidated snowpack buries the ridge brush and corn snow refreezes overnight

December.reason: The snowpack may not yet bury the ridge brush, days are very short and storm cycles load the gully's avalanche paths.

January.reason: Deep but often unconsolidated snow gives poor axe placements, and frequent storms keep the gully's avalanche paths active.

February.reason: A deeper snowpack covers the brush and cliffs on the ridge; climb only in a stable spell after a storm cycle settles.

March.reason: Consolidated snow buries the brush, the constriction is a snow ramp, and longer days fit the long car-to-car climb.

April.reason: Corn snow that refreezes overnight gives the most secure climbing; start very early before sun loosens the east-facing gully.

May.reason: Early May can still be good, but by mid-month wet slides and rockfall in the gully and melting brush on the ridge take over.

June.reason: The gully turns into wet rock and a waterfall, and the melted-out ridge becomes a steep, brushy fifth-class tree climb.

May.reason: Deep, consolidating snow in the couloir; the road gate creeps higher, and a pre-dawn start avoids sun-triggered sluff and rockfall.

June.reason: The couloir is still full, and Cascade River Road usually opens to the trailhead by month's end, removing the road walk.

July.reason: The line thins and melts toward rock, the cliffs on both sides shed rockfall into the funnel, and the Yawning Glacier opens up.

August.reason: Largely melted to loose rock with constant rockfall down the chute; better climbed by the North Face.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, once the road is open and the pocket-glacier bergschrund is still bridged or easily crossed

June.reason: Cascade River Road usually opens only at the end of June, and Cache Col and the pocket glacier are still deep in snow.

July.reason: Road open and the Cache Glacier approach on good snow; the bergschrund is usually well filled, but the open book can still hold snow.

August.reason: Dry rock on the 5.6 open book and slab, with the bergschrund still crossable in most years.

September.reason: Rock stays dry, but the bergschrund below the face widens and the Cache Glacier approach turns icy.

October.reason: An open, awkward bergschrund, early snow on the ledges and short days on a long approach over Cache Col.
